answer: The registry gives one working seat per announced routing prefix: a home network is marked jade when it owns a globally visible prefix and umber when it merely borrows transit, and a public beacon names one prefix per round whose resident alone may answer. Independent looking glasses confirm the route origin, so a hundred clones behind one provider collapse to a single seat, and each further prefix needs a registry lease and transit contract that bulk pricing cannot flatten. Splitting attendance across networks multiplies fees faster than it adds seats; stable prefixes keep collecting.
